column2: What must an emergency deployment process preserve?
column3: Named authority, limited scope, traceability, essential validation and prompt retrospective review.

column2: Which application values should usually vary by deployment environment?
column3: Service endpoints, resource identifiers and operational settings; secret values should use protected delivery mechanisms.

column2: How can the same binary run in different environments without rebuilding?
column3: Supply external configuration at deployment or runtime through an authorised mechanism.

column2: What does a secret reference contain instead of the secret value?
column3: An identifier or locator resolved by an authorised runtime or deployment process.

column2: An operator changes a firewall rule outside IaC. What is this relative to the declared configuration?
column3: Infrastructure drift, requiring assessment and either reconciliation or an authorised configuration update.

column2: Which staging characteristics matter for representative production testing?
column3: Relevant versions, topology, configuration and dependency behaviour, with scale and data differences explicitly accounted for.

column2: What lifecycle controls does an ephemeral preview environment need?
column3: Ownership, isolated access, bounded lifetime, cost controls and cleanup of resources and data.

column2: What protects production deployment authority across execution paths?
column3: Least-privilege identities, protected resources, reviewed definitions, approvals and audit coverage for every permitted route.

column2: What should precede application code that requires a new database column?
column3: A compatible schema expansion, followed by rollout and verification of the new application.

column2: Why is adding an optional column usually safer than immediately renaming a used column?
column3: Old and new application versions can coexist with the optional addition; a rename can break old queries.

column2: What are the phases of expand-and-contract migration?
column3: Add a compatible new interface, migrate consumers and data, then remove the old interface after it is unused.

column2: What additional constraints affect a stateful application rollout?
column3: Persistent-data compatibility, replication and quorum, storage attachment and safe sequencing of readers and writers.

column2: Why may restoring the old application not undo a migration?
column3: Deleted or transformed data and schema changes persist independently of the application binary.

column2: What compatibility must a rolling application/database release preserve?
column3: Every simultaneously running application version must work with the deployed schema and shared data semantics.

column2: What makes a build a release candidate?
column3: It is a specifically identified candidate for release that has met defined preliminary criteria and awaits final acceptance.

column2: Does promotion require recompiling an approved release candidate?
column3: No. Promote the same validated artifact and record its eligibility for the next stage.

column2: What operational details belong in release notes?
column3: Behavioural and compatibility changes, upgrade actions, known issues and relevant recovery implications.

column2: What traceability chain should a public release version have?
column3: Release version to artifact digest, build run and source revision, with provenance for other inputs.

column2: What evidence establishes deployment provenance?
column3: Actor or workload identity, workflow/run, time, target and exact artifact deployed.

column2: What distinguishes a useful change record from a bare deployment timestamp?
column3: It records why the change occurred, its scope, authorisation, validation and outcome.

column2: What should guide rollback during an incident?
column3: Expected restoration of user service, confidence in the causal change, data compatibility and the relative risk of available recovery actions.
